title: One More Time
label: Virgin
note: The lead single from Daft Punk's second album, Discovery, built on a looped horn sample and Romanthony's heavily Auto-Tuned vocal. It took French house out of the clubs and into the charts worldwide, and its pitched-up vocal treatment was copied for the rest of the decade.

title: Around the World
label: Virgin
note: Thomas Bangalter and Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo repeat the title 144 times over a rubbery bassline on this track from their 1997 debut, Homework. Michel Gondry's video, with each dancer group playing one instrument, made it one of the most famous dance records of the 90s.

title: Harder, Better, Faster, Stronger
label: Virgin
note: A Discovery-era track built around a chopped sample of Edwin Birdsong's 1979 song "Cola Bottle Baby". It became even bigger when Kanye West sampled it for "Stronger" in 2007, introducing Daft Punk to a whole new audience.

title: Music Sounds Better With You
label: Roulé
note: A one-off by Thomas Bangalter of Daft Punk, Alan Braxe and singer Benjamin Diamond, released on Bangalter's Roulé label. Built on a loop from Chaka Khan's "Fate", it sold millions and became the template for filtered French disco-house.

title: Show Me Love
label: Champion
note: Robin S's vocal over StoneBridge's remix turned a 1990 R&B single into one of the biggest house records ever. That organ-bass riff, a Korg M1 preset, is among the most sampled and copied sounds in dance music.

title: Gypsy Woman (She's Homeless)
label: Mercury
note: Crystal Waters wrote the lyric about a homeless woman she saw in Washington, D.C., and the Basement Boys produced it. Its "la da dee la dee da" hook made it a global hit in 1991 and showed that a house record could carry a serious story.

title: Finally
label: A&M
note: CeCe Peniston was a student in Phoenix when she wrote and recorded this, her first single. It became one of the defining vocal house anthems of the early 90s and is still a fixture of diva-house sets.

title: Free
label: AM:PM
note: Baltimore singer Ultra Naté's 1997 anthem, co-produced by Mood II Swing. It reached the top five in the UK, and its message of personal freedom made it a staple of Pride celebrations ever since.

title: Don't You Want Me
label: deConstruction
note: Francis Wright made this as Felix and released it on deConstruction in 1992. Its stabbing riff and diva vocal hook took it to number six in the UK, and it became one of the defining house records of the rave era.

title: Pump Up the Jam
label: ARS
note: A Belgian production by Jo Bogaert, with Congolese-born rapper Ya Kid K on vocals; model Felly mimed in the original video. Its hip-house groove crossed over worldwide in 1989 and helped bring house music into pop culture.

title: Ride on Time
label: deConstruction
note: Italo house by the Italian production team Black Box, built around an uncredited sample of Loleatta Holloway's "Love Sensation". It spent six weeks at number one in the UK in 1989, and the dispute that followed sparked a debate about crediting vocalists.

title: Born Slippy (Nuxx)
label: Junior Boy's Own
note: Underworld released this as a B-side in 1995, then it exploded a year later when it soundtracked the closing scene of Trainspotting. The shouted "lager, lager, lager" refrain became a symbol of 90s UK club culture.

title: Where's Your Head At
label: XL Recordings
note: South London duo Felix Buxton and Simon Ratcliffe built this from a heavily processed sample of Gary Numan's "M.E." The video, with monkeys bearing the band members' faces, became an MTV classic, and the track showed how chaotic and punk-influenced house could be.

title: Lady (Hear Me Tonight)
label: Sound of Barclay
note: French duo Modjo looped the guitar riff from Chic's "Soup for One" under Yann Destagnol's vocal. It went to number one in the UK in 2000, one of the last major hits of the filtered French house wave.

title: Go
label: Outer Rhythm
note: Moby's breakthrough single samples the theme from the TV series Twin Peaks over a rave piano. It was a UK top-ten hit in 1991 and helped establish him as a techno artist years before Play made him a household name.

title: Red Alert
label: XL Recordings
note: The first big single from Basement Jaxx's debut album, Remedy. Built from a Locksmith disco sample, it captured the cut-up, anything-goes sound of their Brixton club night Rooty.

title: You Don't Know Me
label: Armed
note: New York producer Armand Van Helden flipped Carrie Lucas's disco track "Dance With You" and added a vocal from Duane Harden. It hit number one in the UK in 1999 and confirmed him as one of the masters of disco-sampling house.

label: Virgin
note: Philippe Zdar and Hubert "Boom Bass" Blanc-Francard, who had worked in hip-hop together, debuted as Cassius with this track. Its sweaty, filtered funk made it one of the key records of the late-90s French touch movement.

title: Big Fun
label: KMS
note: Kevin Saunderson's project with Chicago singer Paris Grey. It reached the UK top ten in 1988 and proved Detroit techno's sound could carry a pop song.

title: Good Life
label: KMS
note: Inner City's biggest hit, released in 1988 and a top-five single in the UK. Kevin Saunderson was one of the Belleville Three who pioneered Detroit techno. This track showed the music's optimism could reach a mass audience.

title: Gold Dust
label: Breakbeat Kaos
note: DJ Fresh's track built around a vocal from dancehall singer Ce'cile, first released in 2008 and a chart hit when reissued in 2010. Its rolling bassline made it a classic of late-2000s drum & bass.

title: Brown Paper Bag
label: Talkin' Loud
note: The standout from Roni Size and Reprazent's New Forms, which won the Mercury Prize in 1997. Its live upright bass and jazz feel showed that drum & bass could be recorded with a band and still hit hard.

title: Inner City Life
label: FFRR
note: Goldie's epic with vocals from Diane Charlemagne, released in 1994 and later the centrepiece of his album Timeless. It blended jungle's breakbeats with soul vocals and lush strings, and is widely seen as the record that made drum & bass an art form.

title: Your Love
label: Trax
note: Written by Jamie Principle and produced by Frankie Knuckles, the "Godfather of House". Its arpeggiated synth line and dreamy feel made it one of the earliest Chicago house classics, played at the Warehouse and the Power Plant in the mid-80s.

title: Voodoo Ray
label: Rham!
note: Gerald Simpson recorded this in Manchester, building the vocal from a sample he cut up and pitched with limited studio gear. One of the first British acid house records, it became an anthem of the Haçienda and the 1988 Second Summer of Love.

title: French Kiss
label: Diamond
note: Chicago producer Lil Louis's ten-minute record that gradually slows to a near-stop before rebuilding, with breathy vocals throughout. It was banned by some radio stations, yet still became a top-three hit in the UK in 1989.

title: Da Funk
label: Soma
note: Daft Punk's first single, released on Glasgow's Soma label in 1995. The squelching, filtered funk riff, made on cheap gear in Thomas Bangalter's bedroom, launched the French house sound and won the duo a major label deal.

title: Higher State of Consciousness
label: Strictly Rhythm
note: Philadelphia producer Josh Wink pushed a Roland TB-303 bassline to screaming intensity on this track. It brought the acid sound to the mainstream in 1995 and became one of the decade's biggest underground-to-chart crossovers.

title: Pump Up the Volume
label: 4AD
note: A one-off collaboration between 4AD bands Colourbox and A.R. Kane, built from dozens of samples. It was the first UK number one built predominantly from samples and became a test case for sampling law.

title: Chime
label: Oh-Zone
note: Brothers Paul and Phil Hartnoll recorded this at home and put it out on the Oh-Zone label in 1990. Its hypnotic chimes made it a rave anthem, and it reached the UK top twenty after being reissued by ffrr, launching Orbital.

title: Halcyon + On + On
label: Internal
note: Orbital wrote this as a tribute to the Hartnolls' mother and her dependence on the tranquiliser Halcion. It samples Opus III and Belinda Carlisle, and its soaring mood made it one of the most emotional techno records ever made.

title: Open Up
label: Hard Hands
note: Leftfield's collaboration with John Lydon, former singer of the Sex Pistols and Public Image Ltd. It fused progressive house with punk snarl in 1993 and became a UK top-twenty hit.

title: Release the Pressure
label: Hard Hands
note: Leftfield's dub-heavy house track featuring vocals from Earl Sixteen. Coming out of London's sound system culture, it showed how British dance music could absorb reggae and dub, a thread that ran through the decade.

title: Move Your Body
label: Trax
note: Marshall Jefferson's 1986 track, also known as "The House Music Anthem". It was one of the first house records to use a piano riff, and that piano became a defining sound of house music.

title: Promised Land
label: DJ International
note: Joe Smooth's 1987 gospel-flavoured house track was a call for unity and hope. It became one of the spiritual anthems of Chicago house and of the UK rave scene.

title: Love Can't Turn Around
label: DJ International
note: Farley "Jackmaster" Funk's cover of Isaac Hayes's "I Can't Turn Around", with Darryl Pandy's huge vocal. Released in 1986, it became one of the first house records to chart in the UK, and its success helped house music spread beyond Chicago.

title: Can You Feel It
label: Trax
note: Larry Heard's deep, melancholic track recorded under the Mr. Fingers alias. Its warm chords and sense of longing invented the deep house template, and it remains one of the most beloved records in house music.

title: Energy Flash
label: R&S
note: New York producer Joey Beltram's 1990 track on Belgium's R&S label. Its hard, distorted rhythm and "ecstasy, ecstasy" whisper influenced hardcore techno and gave journalist Simon Reynolds the title of his book on rave culture.

title: Crispy Bacon
label: F Communications
note: French techno pioneer Laurent Garnier's track from his album 30. Its insistent hammering groove made it a staple in Garnier's DJ sets, which were among the most respected in Europe.

title: Pacific State
label: ZTT
note: Manchester's 808 State took their name from the Roland TR-808 drum machine. This track's saxophone line over a laid-back groove made it a Haçienda anthem in 1989 and one of the first British acid house hits.

title: Get Get Down
label: Moody
note: Chicago producer Paul Johnson's ghetto house track built on a looped disco-funk vocal. It reached the UK top five in 1999 and is one of the most infectious Chicago house records ever.

title: On a Ragga Tip
label: XL Recordings
note: SL2 (Slipmatt and Lime) built this on a ragga vocal sample over breakbeats. A top-three UK hit in 1992, it was among the first ragga-hardcore records to cross over, pointing the way toward jungle.

title: Flash
label: Relief
note: Curtis Jones, recording as Green Velvet, delivers a deadpan spoken warning about partying over a pounding beat. Released on his Relief label in 1995, it became one of the most recognisable tracks in Chicago techno.

title: Camargue
label: R&S
note: Belgian-based producer CJ Bolland's 1992 track built on sweeping strings. Released on R&S, it captured the euphoric side of early-90s European techno and became one of its biggest anthems.

title: Positive Education
label: Soma
note: Glasgow duo Stuart McMillan and Orde Meikle, who also run the Soma label. This 1993 track became an anthem at their Slam club nights and is a foundational record of Scottish techno.

title: Super Sharp Shooter
label: Ganja
note: DJ Zinc's jungle track pairs a hip-hop vocal sample with a booming bassline. Released on Ganja Records in 1995, it became one of the most played jungle records ever.

title: Pull Over
label: Plus 8
note: Dutch producer Jochem Paap recorded this as Speedy J for Richie Hawtin's Plus 8 label in 1991. It connected the European and Detroit techno scenes and helped define Plus 8's high-energy sound.

title: Acperience 1
label: Harthouse
note: German duo Hardfloor built this 1992 track around the Roland TB-303. Its twisting acid lines made it a key record of the acid revival and a touchstone for the Harthouse label.

title: Acid Tracks
label: Trax
note: DJ Pierre, Spanky and Herb J made this with a Roland TB-303 bass synth, twisting its knobs until it squelched. Released on Trax in 1987, it was the first acid house record and gave a whole genre its name.

title: Mr. Kirk's Nightmare
label: Reinforced
note: 4hero's 1990 track on their own Reinforced label tells the story of a parent finding out their child has died of an overdose. With its breakbeats and sub-bass it was an early example of the dark side of hardcore that would become jungle.

title: Rain
note: New Jersey producer Kerri Chandler is one of the leading figures of deep house. This 1998 track's lush chords and live feel became a model for soulful house.

title: That's the Way Love Is
label: Atlantic
note: Chicago group Ten City, with Byron Stingily's falsetto vocal, produced by Marshall Jefferson. It showed that house music could be soulful and song-based, setting the tone for decades of vocal house.

title: Spastik
label: Plus 8
note: Richie Hawtin's track as Plastikman, released on Plus 8 in 1993. It uses almost nothing but drum machine sounds pushed through effects, yet sounds huge, and became a landmark of minimal techno.

title: The Bells
label: Purpose Maker
note: Jeff Mills, a founding member of Underground Resistance, released this on his Purpose Maker label in 1997. Its hypnotic bell melody and relentless drive made it one of techno's most famous peak-time records.

title: Clear
label: Fantasy
note: Juan Atkins and Rick Davis's 1983 track as Cybotron. Its robotic electro funk, influenced by Kraftwerk, directly led to Detroit techno, and it is often cited as one of the genre's foundation stones.

title: No UFO's
label: Metroplex
note: Juan Atkins, the "Originator" of techno, released this as Model 500 on his Metroplex label in 1985. It was a key early techno record, using electronic sounds to create a futuristic Detroit funk.

title: LFO
label: Warp
note: Leeds duo LFO's 1990 debut on Sheffield's Warp label. Its earth-shaking bass made it a top-twenty hit and defined bleep techno, the first distinctively British form of techno.

title: Altered States
label: Warehouse
note: Ron Trent recorded this in Chicago as a teenager, and it came out on the Warehouse label in 1990. Its moody, spacious sound made it one of the most respected deep house records of all time.

title: Shades of Jae
label: KDJ
note: Detroit producer Kenny Dixon Jr., known as Moodymann, released this on his KDJ label. His sample-heavy, soulful approach made him one of the most distinctive voices in deep house.

title: Land of Confusion
label: Warehouse
note: Chicago producer Armando Gallop's 1988 track on Warehouse is one of the darkest early acid house records. Armando died in 1996 at the age of 26, and he remains a cult figure in Chicago house.

title: Knights of the Jaguar
label: Underground Resistance
note: Originally released by Underground Resistance under DJ Rolando's alias The Aztec Mystic in 1998. Its melancholic synth line made it a global techno anthem, and UR famously fought a major label's attempt to cover it.

title: Valley of the Shadows
label: Ram
note: Andy C and Ant Miles released this as Origin Unknown on their Ram label in 1993. Its ominous atmosphere and rolling breaks made it a jungle landmark, and Ram became one of drum & bass's most powerful labels.

title: Call & Response
note: Phil Aslett and Jim Baker, as Source Direct, made some of the darkest, most technically ambitious drum & bass of the 90s. This 1997 track shows their cinematic tension and precise drum programming.

title: Here Comes the Drumz
note: Doc Scott's 1992 track helped lay the foundations for the dark side of jungle. Scott was a central figure at Metalheadz, the label and club night that defined serious drum & bass.

title: Minus
label: M-Plant
note: Robert Hood, a founding member of Underground Resistance, released this on his M-Plant label in 1994. His stripped-back approach on records like Minimal Nation helped invent minimal techno.

title: The Angels Fell
label: Metalheadz
note: Dillinja, a South London producer famous for some of the heaviest basslines in drum & bass, released this on Goldie's Metalheadz label. Its mix of melancholy and pressure made it a classic of the mid-90s scene.

title: R.I.P.
label: Suburban Base
note: Remarc was known for intricate breakbeat edits, and this 1994 track shows his precise, cut-up drum programming. It became a classic of the ragga-jungle era.

title: Renegade Snares
label: Moving Shadow
note: Rob Haigh's project Omni Trio released this on Moving Shadow in 1993. Its combination of piano, soulful vocals and breakbeats helped bridge hardcore and the more melodic drum & bass that followed.

title: At Les
label: Planet E
note: Detroit producer Carl Craig released this on his album More Songs About Food and Revolutionary Art. Its reflective atmosphere showed techno could be contemplative, influencing generations of electronic artists.

title: Digital Love
label: Virgin
note: A Discovery-era song about a dream romance, built on soft-rock and disco influences. Its vocoder vocal and long solo made it one of the album's best-loved tracks, and one of Daft Punk's most romantic.

title: Revolution 909
label: Virgin
note: Daft Punk's single from Homework opens with a police raid shutting down a party. It was a sly commentary on France's crackdown on raves in the mid-90s.

title: Robot Rock
label: Virgin
note: The lead single from Daft Punk's 2005 album Human After All, built on a sample of Breakwater's "Release the Beast". Its heavy guitar sound pointed toward the rock-influenced electro of the late 2000s.

title: Burnin'
label: Virgin
note: A Homework-era single with a pumping, filtered loop. It showcases the raw, distorted sound Daft Punk used to bring French house to clubs around the world.

title: Rollin' & Scratchin'
label: Soma
note: Released on Soma alongside Da Funk in 1995, this is the closest Daft Punk came to pure techno. Its grinding, distorted loops show their roots in raves and in Chicago acid.

title: Technologic
label: Virgin
note: From Daft Punk's Human After All, its robotic vocal lists commands for using technology. The repetitive minimalism of the album polarised critics on release but influenced the electro scene that followed.

title: Romeo
label: XL Recordings
note: Basement Jaxx's single with Kele Le Roc on vocals, from their 2001 album Rooty. It became a top-ten UK hit and showed the duo could write pop songs without losing their South London club roots.

title: Rendez-Vu
label: XL Recordings
note: A Latin-flavoured, guitar-driven single from Basement Jaxx's debut album Remedy. It was a UK top-five hit in 1999 and helped define their eclectic, party-first take on house.

title: Fly Life
label: Multiply
note: Basement Jaxx's 1997 single, which came out of their South London club night Rooty. Its raw energy and vocal hooks made it their first club smash, years before mainstream success.

title: My My My
label: Southern Fried
note: Armand Van Helden's 2004 track built on a looped rock guitar riff, released on the London label Southern Fried. It was a club smash and a UK chart hit, and kept him at the top of the house world into the 2000s.

title: Groovejet (If This Ain't Love)
label: Positiva
note: Italian producer Cristiano Spiller's track with Sophie Ellis-Bextor on vocals, built on a sample of Carol Williams's "Love Is You". It hit number one in the UK in 2000, beating Victoria Beckham to the top in a famously publicised chart battle.

title: Another Chance
label: Defected
note: New York DJ Roger Sanchez's single went to number one in the UK in 2001. It sampled Toto's "I Won't Hold You Back" and became one of the defining hits of the early-2000s house boom.

title: E Samba
label: Defected
note: Vito Lucente's track as Junior Jack, built on a Latin percussion groove. Released on Defected, it became one of the label's defining records of the early 2000s.

title: Horny
label: Peppermint Jam
note: German producer Mousse T's track with Hot 'n' Juicy on vocals. It reached the UK top five in 1998, and its cheeky disco-house bounce made it one of the decade's most played party records.

title: Put Your Hands Up for Detroit
label: Flamingo
note: Dutch producer Fedde Le Grand built this around a vocal loop from Scott Grooves's "Mothership Reconnection". Its stripped, bouncy sound went to number one in the UK in 2006 and became an anthem of the electro house boom.

title: Pjanoo
label: Data
note: Swedish producer Eric Prydz's piano-led instrumental reached number two in the UK in 2008. It showed that a wordless club track could still become a mainstream pop hit.

title: Turn Around
label: Multiply
note: Brighton duo Phats & Small built this around Toney Lee's 1983 boogie track "Reach Up". A UK top-ten hit in 1999, it captured the era of upbeat, disco-sampling house.

title: King of My Castle
label: Strictly Rhythm
note: Chris Brann's project Wamdue Project released this in 1997, but its Roy Malone remix made it a UK number one in 1999. Its melancholic vocal set it apart from typical house hits.

title: Make Luv
label: Positiva
note: Belgian producer Junior Jack's project Room 5 used a vocal from Oliver Cheatham's "Get Down Saturday Night". It was a UK number one in 2003 after being used in a TV advert for Lynx.

title: Superstylin'
label: Pepper
note: Groove Armada's single from their 2001 album Goodbye Country (Hello Nightclub), with vocals from MC M.A.D. Its funky, bass-heavy groove made it a festival favourite for years.

title: In My Arms
label: Breastfed
note: Scottish producer Mylo made his album Destroy Rock & Roll on a laptop in his bedroom. This track, which samples Boy Meets Girl and Kim Carnes, became one of the biggest dance hits of 2004–05.

title: Finally
label: Distance
note: New Jersey's Kings of Tomorrow, led by Sandy Rivera, released this soulful vocal house track featuring Julie McKnight in 2000. It became one of the most loved soulful house records of the decade.

title: Dreamer
label: Undiscovered
note: Italian production team Livin' Joy, with American singer Janice Robinson on vocals. It reached number one in the UK in 1995 and became one of the key songs of mid-90s Italo house.

title: The Bomb! (These Sounds Fall Into My Mind)
label: Henry Street
note: The Bucketheads was a project of Masters at Work's Kenny "Dope" Gonzalez. Built from a sample of Chicago's "Street Player", it became one of the most popular disco-sampling house records of the 90s.

title: Hey Hey
label: Objektivity
note: New York producer Dennis Ferrer's track with vocals by Mia Tuttavilla. Released on his Objektivity label, it became one of the biggest club anthems of 2009 and later crossed into the UK charts.

title: The Whistle Song
label: Virgin
note: Frankie Knuckles's 1991 track with its distinctive flute-like whistle melody. It topped the US dance chart and showed the gentler, more musical side of house.

title: Rhythm Is a Mystery
label: deConstruction
note: K-Klass, from Wales and North West England, released this in 1991 with a vocal from Bobbi Depasois. Its piano and rave energy made it an anthem of early-90s British house.

title: The Sun Rising
label: WEA
note: The Beloved's 1989 single was inspired by the ambient and Balearic sounds of the Second Summer of Love. Its blissful mood made it a classic of the chill-out room.

title: Can You Party
label: Idlers
note: Todd Terry's 1988 track as Royal House, with its "Can you party?" chant. Terry's sample-driven style fused hip-hop and house and was hugely influential on the UK rave scene.

title: Beautiful People
label: Strictly Rhythm
note: Barbara Tucker's 1994 single became one of the classic vocal house tracks of the 90s. Tucker went on to be one of the leading voices of New York house.

title: Someday
label: Atlantic
note: Ce Ce Rogers's vocal over a Marshall Jefferson production. Released in 1987, its gospel-tinged plea for a better world made it a key early house song.

title: Plastic Dreams
label: R&S
note: Dutch DJ Robin Albers's 1992 track as Jaydee. Released on R&S, its organ-driven groove made it a crossover anthem in house and techno clubs.

title: Get Up (Everybody)
label: Nervous
note: Ten City's former lead singer Byron Stingily went solo with this 1997 track. Its falsetto vocal and celebratory feel made it a classic of late-90s vocal house.

title: Rej
label: Sonar Kollektiv
note: German duo Âme's 2005 track became a defining record of the mid-2000s deep house and tech house sound. Its hypnotic loop crossed over from underground to the mainstream.

title: Sky and Sand
label: BPitch Control
note: German producer Paul Kalkbrenner's track from the film Berlin Calling, in which he also starred. Its melodic techno sound became an anthem of Berlin club culture in the late 2000s.

title: Gabriel
label: Large
note: Chicago producer Roy Davis Jr.'s track with Peven Everett's vocal mixes soulful house and UK garage. It became one of the foundational records of the UK garage scene in 1997.

title: No Way Back
label: Trax
note: Adonis's 1986 track on Trax was one of the first Chicago house records to explore a darker, more hypnotic feel. Its dry drum machine and bass made it a blueprint for acid house.

title: Mystery of Love
label: Alleviated
note: Larry Heard, recording as Mr. Fingers, released this in 1985–86, around the same time as "Can You Feel It". Its lush feel made it one of the founding records of deep house.

title: Rich in Paradise
label: Rumour
note: Italian group FPI Project released this Italo house track in 1989. Its piano riff and diva vocal helped define the sound of Italo house that dominated European clubs at the turn of the decade.

title: I'll Be Your Friend
label: Play It Again Sam
note: Robert Owens, whose voice graced many early Chicago house records, released this in 1991 with a Def Mix production by Frankie Knuckles and David Morales. It became a classic of New York-style vocal house.

title: The Nervous Track
label: Nervous
note: Masters at Work, Louie Vega and Kenny "Dope" Gonzalez, recorded this 1993 track as Nuyorican Soul. Its percussion-heavy groove is a template for the Latin-tinged New York house sound.

title: Beau Mot Plage
label: Classic
note: German producer Rajko Müller's track as Isolée, released in 2000. Its intricate, playful sound is one of the founding records of microhouse.

title: Moan
label: Poker Flat
note: Danish producer Anders Trentemøller's 2006 track on Poker Flat. Its dark, cinematic sound helped define the moody, melodic minimal techno of the mid-2000s.

title: Washing Machine
label: Trax
note: Larry Heard's 1986 Mr. Fingers track on Trax. Its raw, jacking feel, made with a basic drum machine and synth, is a perfect example of Chicago house in its earliest form.

title: Where's Your Child?
label: Westbrook
note: Chicago producer Bam Bam's 1988 track. Its dark, eerie mood and spoken vocal made it a cult classic and one of the most unusual early acid house records.

title: Acid Thunder
label: DJ International
note: Chicago's Fast Eddie released this on DJ International in 1988. Its relentless 303 line made it one of the most influential early acid house records.

title: I've Lost Control
label: Trax
note: Sleezy D's 1986 track, produced by Marshall Jefferson, is often cited as one of the first acid house records. Its eerie vocal and squelching bass made it one of Chicago's darkest early tracks.

title: Barefoot in the Head
label: Acid Jazz
note: A Man Called Adam's 1990 track blends jazz, house and Balearic sounds. It became a classic of the post-Second Summer of Love chill-out era.

title: Here's Your Trance, Now Dance!!
label: FXHE
note: Detroit producer Alex "Omar S" Smith releases music on his own FXHE label. This 2005 track's raw, uncompromising sound made him one of the most celebrated house producers of the 2000s.

title: Rez
label: Junior Boy's Own
note: Underworld's 1993 track is a nine-minute build of synth arpeggios. It showed techno could be both hypnotic and euphoric, and became a festival anthem.

title: Cowgirl
label: Junior Boy's Own
note: The 1994 track from Underworld's album dubnobasswithmyheadman. Karl Hyde's cryptic vocals and Rick Smith's building synths made it one of their most beloved live songs.

title: King of Snake
label: Junior Boy's Own
note: Underworld's 1999 single from Beaucoup Fish. It reportedly samples Donna Summer's "I Feel Love" bassline, nodding to one of dance music's founding records.

title: Two Months Off
label: Junior Boy's Own
note: Underworld's 2002 single from A Hundred Days Off, with its gospel-like chorus. It showed the band evolving after Darren Emerson's departure.

title: Belfast
label: ffrr
note: Orbital's track from their 1991 debut album (known as the Green Album). Its gentle, ambient-tinged mood made it a classic of the British techno that was emerging from the rave scene.

title: Song of Life
label: Hard Hands
note: Leftfield's 1992 track on their own Hard Hands label. Its dub-influenced progressive house sound helped define British dance music in the early 90s.

title: The Man With the Red Face
label: F Communications
note: Laurent Garnier's 2000 track built around a saxophone improvisation. It became one of the most played techno records of the decade, showing how jazz could fit into techno.

title: Anthem
label: deConstruction
note: N-Joi's 1990 track on deConstruction was one of the defining rave anthems. Its piano and vocal sample captured the euphoric energy of UK raves.

title: Playing With Knives
label: Vinyl Solution
note: Bizarre Inc's 1991 rave track on Vinyl Solution. Its piano riff and vocal made it a top-five hit and one of the classic British rave records.

title: Dominator
label: R&S
note: Dutch project Human Resource released this in 1991 on R&S. Its harsh, buzzing "Hoover" sound made it one of the founding records of hardcore techno.

title: Anasthasia
label: XL Recordings
note: Belgian project T99 released this in 1991. Its harsh synth riff made it a key track of the Belgian new beat and hardcore sound.

title: Digeridoo
label: R&S
note: Richard D. James, as Aphex Twin, released this in 1992 on R&S. Its frantic, distorted energy made it one of the most loved early 90s rave records and showed his range before his move into IDM.

title: Mentasm
label: R&S
note: Joey Beltram's 1991 track as Second Phase. Its howling, distorted synth sound, known as the Hoover, became the defining sound of early-90s hardcore.

title: Throw
label: Planet E
note: Carl Craig's 1994 track as Paperclip People. Its disco-sampling, groove-based sound bridged house and techno and became a classic in both scenes.

title: Blackwater
label: 430 West
note: Detroit's Octave One, the Burden brothers, released this in 2000 with a vocal from Ann Saunderson. It became one of the biggest techno crossover hits of the decade.

title: Alleys of Your Mind
label: Deep Space
note: Cybotron's 1981 debut single. Juan Atkins and Rick Davis's dark, synth-driven sound was one of the first steps toward Detroit techno.

title: Techno City
label: Fantasy
note: Cybotron's 1984 track named after their vision of Detroit's future. It is one of the earliest records to put the word techno at the heart of Detroit's electronic sound.

title: Night Drive (Thru-Babylon)
label: Metroplex
note: Juan Atkins's 1985 track as Model 500. Its futuristic electro funk helped lay the foundations for the Detroit techno sound.

title: Groove La Chord
label: Fragile
note: Swedish producer Aril Brikha's 1998 track, released on the Detroit label Fragile. Its soaring chords made it one of the most beloved Detroit-style techno records.

title: Testone
label: Warp
note: Richard H. Kirk of Cabaret Voltaire and DJ Parrot recorded this as Sweet Exorcist. Released on Warp in 1990, it is one of the founding records of Sheffield's bleep techno.

title: Aftermath
label: Warp
note: Leeds group Nightmares on Wax released this on Warp in 1990. Its bleep sound and heavy bass made it one of the label's earliest classics.

title: The Theme
label: Ten
note: Bradford group Unique 3 released this in 1989. Its sub-bass and bleeps made it one of the first records of the UK bleep techno sound.

title: Charly
label: XL Recordings
note: The Prodigy's 1991 breakthrough samples a cat's meow from a 1970s British public information film. It was a top-three UK hit, and its success sparked a wave of "toytown techno" built on children's TV samples.

title: Out of Space
label: XL Recordings
note: The Prodigy's 1992 single samples Max Romeo's reggae song "Chase the Devil". Its mix of breakbeats, reggae and rave sounds became one of the defining records of UK hardcore.

title: Everybody in the Place
label: XL Recordings
note: The Prodigy's 1992 single, their biggest of the rave era, reached number two in the UK. Its frantic breakbeats and piano riffs captured hardcore at its peak.

title: Incredible
label: Renk
note: M-Beat's 1994 track with ragga vocalist General Levy reached the UK top ten. It was one of the first jungle records to cross into the mainstream, though Levy's comments in the press caused a backlash in the scene.

title: Let Me Be Your Fantasy
label: Production House
note: Baby D's track came out in 1992 and became a breakbeat hardcore anthem, then reached number one in the UK when it was reissued at the start of 1995. It is one of the biggest records to come out of the London rave scene.

title: Sesame's Treet
label: Suburban Base
note: Smart E's took the Sesame Street theme and put it over rave breakbeats in 1992. It reached number two in the UK and is the most famous example of the toytown techno craze.

title: Tarantula
label: Breakbeat Kaos
note: Australian group Pendulum's 2005 single with Fresh and Spyda. Its rock-influenced, high-energy sound helped bring drum & bass to festival main stages.

title: Eastern Jam
label: RAM
note: Chase & Status's 2008 track sets an Eastern vocal sample over heavy drum & bass. It became an anthem of the late-2000s era when drum & bass and dubstep began crossing over.

title: Rock It
label: RAM
note: Sub Focus's track on Andy C's Ram label. Its stadium-sized synth sound made Sub Focus one of the most popular drum & bass producers of the late 2000s.

title: Sweet Harmony
label: XL Recordings
note: Liquid's 1992 breakbeat hardcore anthem, made by Shaun Imrei and Eamon Downes, reached the UK top twenty. Its piano and vocal captured the euphoric side of rave.

title: Timeless
label: FFRR
note: The 21-minute title track from Goldie's 1995 debut album, a three-part symphony that includes Inner City Life. The album proved drum & bass could work as a serious long-form art form.

title: Up All Night
label: Beta
note: British producer John B's 2006 track. Its electro-influenced style made it a crossover hit and showed how drum & bass absorbed influences from other scenes in the 2000s.

title: Racing Green
label: Hospital
note: Welsh producer Lincoln Barrett's track as High Contrast, from his 2002 debut album on Hospital Records. Its uplifting, disco-sampling sound helped define liquid funk.

title: Took My Love
label: Vinyl Solution
note: Bizarre Inc's 1993 single with Angie Brown on vocals reached the UK top ten. It marked the shift from rave to more vocal, house-based anthems.

title: Tribal Base
label: Desire
note: Rebel MC, real name Michael West, released this in 1991 with Barrington Levy and Tenor Fly. Mixing reggae with breakbeats, it was one of the first records to point toward jungle.

title: Bombscare
label: Moving Shadow
note: 2 Bad Mice's 1991 track on Moving Shadow. Its chopped breakbeats and energy made it a defining record of early UK hardcore.

title: Rainbows of Colour
label: Higher Ground
note: Grooverider, one of the pioneering DJs of jungle and drum & bass, released this in 1998. He and Fabio ran the influential Rage club night and later had shows on BBC Radio 1.

title: Return of Forever
label: Hospital
note: High Contrast's track blending soulful vocals with rolling drum & bass. It became one of the best-known anthems of the liquid funk style.

title: Atlantis (I Need You)
label: Good Looking
note: LTJ Bukem's 1993 track on his Good Looking label. Its jazz-tinged, atmospheric sound helped create the melodic, ambient side of drum & bass, known as intelligent drum & bass.

title: The Hidden Camera
label: Science
note: Photek, real name Rupert Parkes, made some of the most intricate drum programming in drum & bass. This 1996 track shows his precise, minimal style.

title: Lord of the Null Lines
label: Moving Shadow
note: Hyper-On Experience, Danny Demierre and Alex Banks, released this on Moving Shadow in 1993. Its intricate breakbeats made it a foundational record of the transition from hardcore to jungle.

title: We Are i.e.
label: i.e. Records
note: Lennie De Ice's 1991 track is often cited as one of the very first jungle records. Its rolling breakbeats and deep bass laid the groundwork for the genre.

title: Silver Blade
label: Metalheadz
note: Dillinja's 1995 track on Metalheadz showcases his huge, distorted basslines. It was a key record of the mid-90s drum & bass scene.

title: Urban Style Music
note: South London producer Lemon D's track blends jazz influences with heavy drums. It is a classic of the mid-90s Metalheadz era.

title: Aerodynamic
label: Virgin
note: A track from Daft Punk's 2001 album Discovery, with a bell intro and a baroque-style guitar solo. Its fusion of rock and electronic sounds was a key feature of the album.

title: The Funk Phenomena
label: Henry Street
note: Armand Van Helden's 1996 track, whose chunky, bass-heavy groove was a staple of mid-90s UK clubs. It was a big influence on the sound that became speed garage.

title: Feeling So Real
label: Mute
note: Moby's 1994 single fuses breakbeats, rave synths and a soulful vocal. It was a UK top-thirty hit and one of the highlights of his album Everything Is Wrong.

title: Satan
label: ffrr
note: Orbital's 1991 track samples the Butthole Surfers. Its harsh, punk-influenced energy contrasted with their gentler work and made it a live favourite for decades.

title: Pearl's Girl
label: Junior Boy's Own
note: Underworld's 1996 single, whose shouted vocal and pounding beat made it a live highlight. It came out the same year Born Slippy made the band famous.

title: Afro-Left
label: Hard Hands
note: A track from Leftfield's 1995 debut album Leftism, featuring Djum Djum's vocal. Its African influence and deep groove made it a favourite of the album's fans.

title: No Good (Start the Dance)
label: XL Recordings
note: The Prodigy's 1994 single samples Kelly Charles's "You're No Good for Me". It reached number four in the UK and marked the band's move from rave to a harder, more song-based sound.

title: Cubik
label: ZTT
note: 808 State's 1990 single with a heavy, grinding synth riff. It reached the UK top ten and became a rave anthem.

title: Something Good
label: ffrr
note: Leeds duo Utah Saints built this on a sample of Kate Bush's "Cloudbusting". A UK top-five hit in 1992, it became one of the defining rave crossover records.

title: Club Lonely
label: Epic
note: Lil Louis's 1992 single with vocals from Joi Cardwell. It showed his range beyond French Kiss and became a key track in the early-90s house scene.

title: 100% Pure Love
label: Mercury
note: Crystal Waters's 1994 follow-up to Gypsy Woman. It was a top-twenty US hit and showed vocal house could thrive in the American pop mainstream.

title: Get Up! (Before the Night Is Over)
label: ARS
note: Technotronic's 1990 follow-up to Pump Up the Jam, with Ya Kid K on vocals. It was another global hit and cemented the group's hip-house sound.

title: Everybody Everybody
label: deConstruction
note: Black Box's 1990 single, again using an uncredited Martha Wash vocal, reached the US top ten. The lawsuit Wash later brought helped change crediting practices for vocalists.

title: Feeling for You
label: Virgin
note: Cassius's 1999 single built on a sample of Gwen McCrae's "All This Love That I'm Givin'". Its warm, filtered sound made it one of the best-loved records of French touch.

title: Something Goin' On
label: Manifesto
note: Todd Terry's 1997 single with vocals from Martha Wash and Jocelyn Brown. It was a UK top-five hit and showed his staying power a decade after Royal House.

title: Bug in the Bassbin
label: Planet E
note: Carl Craig's 1992 track as Innerzone Orchestra blends jazz and breakbeats. It influenced early drum & bass producers, a rare Detroit record to cross into the UK jungle scene.

title: Bubble Metropolis
label: Underground Resistance
note: Detroit duo Drexciya, James Stinson and Gerald Donald, released this on Underground Resistance in 1993. Their electro built a mythology of an underwater nation descended from enslaved Africans.

title: Beautiful Life
label: Kompakt
note: Brazilian producer Gui Boratto's 2007 track on Cologne's Kompakt label. Its melodic, emotional sound made it a defining record of the late-2000s minimal and melodic techno scene.

title: Angel
label: FFRR
note: A track from Goldie's 1995 album Timeless. Its dark, brooding mood showed the emotional depth drum & bass could reach.

title: If We Ever
label: Hospital
note: High Contrast's track from his 2007 album Tough Guys Don't Dance, built around a soulful vocal hook over rolling drums. It became a staple of the late-2000s liquid drum & bass scene.

title: X-Ray
label: RAM
note: Sub Focus's 2005 track on Ram Records. Its dark, techy sound helped launch his career as one of drum & bass's leading producers.

title: Music
label: Good Looking
note: LTJ Bukem's 1993 track, a showcase for his jazzy, ambient style. Released on his Good Looking label, it helped define the atmospheric side of drum & bass.

title: Some Justice
label: Urban Shakedown
note: Urban Shakedown, featuring Micky Finn, built this 1991 hardcore track on the vocal from Ce Ce Rogers's "Someday". Its breakbeats and bass made it an early classic that pointed the way to jungle.

title: Dred Bass
label: Moving Shadow
note: Dead Dred's 1994 track on Moving Shadow. Its booming bass and ragga influences made it a jungle classic.

title: Fire
label: XL Recordings
note: The Prodigy's 1992 single samples Arthur Brown's "Fire". Its rave energy and rock sample hinted at the band's future direction.

title: Next Is the E
label: Instinct
note: Moby's 1992 track showcases his early rave sound. Its euphoric energy made it one of his key early club tracks.

title: Sound of Eden
label: ZTT
note: Shades of Rhythm's 1991 track on ZTT. Its rave sound made it a top-twenty UK hit and a key record of the era.

title: Pennies From Heaven
label: Ten
note: Inner City's 1992 single with Paris Grey on vocals. It showed Kevin Saunderson's ability to blend Detroit techno with pop songwriting.

title: The Chase
label: Metroplex
note: Juan Atkins's 1989 single as Model 500, released on his own Metroplex label. Its driving, futuristic sound shows Detroit techno growing out of its electro roots into something faster and harder.

title: Cosmic Cars
label: Deep Space
note: Cybotron's 1982 follow-up to Alleys of Your Mind. Juan Atkins and Rick Davis's robotic electro about cars and the future, a nod to the Motor City, laid more of the groundwork for Detroit techno.

title: Goodbye Kiss
label: Metroplex
note: Eddie "Flashin" Fowlkes, an early associate of Juan Atkins and Kevin Saunderson, released this on Atkins's Metroplex label in 1986. It's one of the first Detroit techno records made by someone outside the founding trio.

title: Rock to the Beat
label: KMS
note: Kevin Saunderson's 1989 track under his Reese alias, released on his KMS label. Raw and stripped back, it shows the hard, bass-heavy side of the Detroit sound that UK rave producers devoured.

title: The Groove That Won't Stop
label: KMS
note: An early Kevin Saunderson record on KMS, the label he founded in 1987. Its relentless drum-machine groove helped define the dancefloor side of Detroit techno.

title: Velocity Funk
label: KMS
note: Kevin Saunderson's 1998 track as E-Dancer. Its heavy, rolling groove became a peak-time techno staple and showed one of Detroit's originators still making some of the genre's biggest records a decade on.

title: Sandstorms
label: Planet E
note: Carl Craig's 1996 track on his Planet E label. Its slowly building, intricate percussion shows his experimental side, and it remains one of the most celebrated Detroit records of the 90s.

title: The Climax
label: Planet E
note: Carl Craig's 1995 track as Paperclip People, built from a looping disco sample. It was a crossover club hit in the UK and showed how Detroit techno could fold disco back into the mix.

title: Tedra
label: Warp
note: Detroit producer Kenny Larkin's track from his 1994 debut album Azimuth, released on Warp. Its lush, melodic style made him one of the leading figures of Detroit techno's second wave.

title: I Believe
note: The 1990 debut of Octave One, the Burden brothers from Detroit. Its soulful, hopeful feel captured the emotional heart of Detroit techno's second wave.

title: Sonic Destroyer
label: Tresor
note: Jeff Mills, Mike Banks and Robert Hood of Underground Resistance recorded this as X-101. It was the very first release on Berlin's Tresor label in 1991, forging the Detroit–Berlin connection that shaped techno for decades.

title: Game One
note: Juan Atkins used the Infiniti name for his more stripped-back, hypnotic records. This mid-90s track shows techno's originator still pushing the sound forward a decade after he started.

title: Direct Drive
label: Direct Beat
note: Detroit group Aux 88 kept electro alive in the city through the 90s. This track's robotic rhythms and booming bass carried the Cybotron tradition to a new generation.

title: Aquabahn
label: Submerge
note: Drexciya's title nods to Kraftwerk's "Autobahn", but moved underwater. Like all the duo's work, it feeds their mythology of a hidden ocean civilisation, showing how Detroit electro could carry a whole story.

title: Sound of Stereo
label: Metroplex
note: Juan Atkins released this as Model 500 in 1987 on Metroplex, his own label and the first Detroit techno label. Having already co-founded Cybotron, Atkins used Model 500 to strip electro down into the cold, rhythmic machine music that became techno.

title: R-9
label: Fantasy
note: A 1985 single from Cybotron, the Detroit duo of Juan Atkins and Rick Davis. Its fast, vocoder-touched electro points toward the machine funk Atkins would develop on his own as Model 500.

title: The Sound
label: KMS
note: Kevin Saunderson, recording as Reese, made this with Santonio Echols for his own KMS label in 1987. With little more than drum machine and stabs, it is Detroit techno at its rawest, from the same years Saunderson was also making hits as Inner City.

title: Pump the Move
label: KMS
note: E-Dancer was the Kevin Saunderson alias he kept for harder, darker club tracks, released on his KMS label. Pump the Move is a stripped-down DJ tool, and the E-Dancer name later carried his 1998 album Heavenly.

title: Suspiria
label: Planet E
note: From More Songs About Food and Revolutionary Art, Carl Craig's 1997 album on his own Planet E label. It shows how Detroit's second generation pushed techno toward moodier, more cinematic home listening.

title: Crackdown
label: Transmat
note: One of Carl Craig's earliest records, made as Psyche and released on Transmat in 1990. Its dark, slow-burning synths announced the producer who would become the leading figure of Detroit's second wave.

title: Remake
label: Planet E
note: Paperclip People was the Carl Craig alias where he looped disco and funk into long, hypnotic grooves for Planet E. Remake runs for more than fifteen minutes and was built for DJs to mix slowly, sitting between Detroit techno and house.

title: People Make the World Go Round
label: Talkin' Loud
note: Carl Craig's Innerzone Orchestra, which played techno with live jazz musicians, covering the Stylistics' 1971 soul song. It comes from the 1999 album Programmed, Craig's most ambitious attempt to fuse Detroit electronics with jazz.

title: Condor to Mallorca
label: Tresor
note: From Waveform Transmission Vol. 3, Jeff Mills's 1994 album for Berlin's Tresor label. After leaving Underground Resistance, Mills built a style of relentless, looping, fast techno, and his Tresor records made him a reference point for DJs worldwide.

title: Changes of Life
label: Tresor
note: From Waveform Transmission Vol. 1, Jeff Mills's 1992 debut album for Berlin's Tresor label. It helped cement the Detroit–Berlin connection, and its hypnotic loop is one of the most played tracks in his catalogue.

title: Museum
label: Axis
note: From Minimal Nation, Robert Hood's 1994 record on Jeff Mills's Axis label. Hood, an original Underground Resistance member, cut techno down to a few repeating parts, and Minimal Nation is widely credited as the starting point of minimal techno.

title: Rhythm of Vision
label: Axis
note: Another track from Robert Hood's 1994 Minimal Nation on Axis. Hood said he wanted to strip techno back to its skeleton after the excesses of early-90s rave, and records like this became the template for minimal techno.

title: Jupiter Jazz
label: Underground Resistance
note: From Underground Resistance's early-90s Galaxy 2 Galaxy era, when Mike Banks's collective fused Detroit techno with jazz chords and funk. It proved the militant, faceless UR could also be lush and melodic.

title: Amazon
label: Underground Resistance
note: An early Underground Resistance record on the collective's own label. UR, led by Mike Banks with Jeff Mills and Robert Hood in its early years, released music anonymously and framed it as resistance against the mainstream music industry.

title: Punisher
label: Underground Resistance
note: One of Underground Resistance's harsh early records from 1991, when Mike Banks and Jeff Mills were making some of the fastest, most abrasive techno in the world. Records like this fed straight into the European hard techno scene.

title: Riot
label: Underground Resistance
note: The title track of Underground Resistance's 1991 Riot EP. UR, led by Mike Banks with Jeff Mills, presented techno as a militant, anonymous movement, and Riot is the collective at its hardest.

title: Andreaen Sand Dunes
label: Tresor
note: From Neptune's Lair, Drexciya's 1999 album for Tresor. The anonymous Detroit duo of James Stinson and Gerald Donald built a mythology of an underwater nation descended from enslaved Africans thrown overboard, told entirely through electro.

title: Java
label: R&S
note: From Metaphor, Kenny Larkin's 1995 album on the Belgian label R&S. Larkin was one of the Detroit producers championed early by Richie Hawtin's Plus 8 label, and Metaphor shows his jazzier, more spacious side.

title: Azimuth
label: Warp
note: From Azimuth, Kenny Larkin's 1994 debut album on Warp. It arrived as Warp was pushing electronic music as something to sit and listen to, and showed Detroit techno could work at album length.

title: Air
label: Transmat
note: Stacey Pullen as Silent Phase, from his 1995 album The Theory Of on Transmat. Pullen was a key figure in Detroit's second wave, and Silent Phase was his deepest, most percussive project.

title: When We Used to Play
label: KMS
note: Blake Baxter's 1987 single on Kevin Saunderson's KMS label. Baxter was part of Detroit's first wave, and his half-sung, soulful vocals over drum machines gave early techno a more personal voice.

title: The Art of Stalking
label: Transmat
note: James Pennington as Suburban Knight, released on Transmat in 1990. Its dark, menacing groove made it a Detroit cult record, and Pennington later worked closely with Underground Resistance.

title: Jazz Is the Teacher
label: Tresor
note: A 1992 Tresor collaboration between Detroit's Juan Atkins and Berlin's Moritz von Oswald and Thomas Fehlmann. It was one of the key records linking Detroit and Berlin, and von Oswald went on to co-found Basic Channel.

title: I Can't Kick This Feelin' When It Hits
label: Planet E
note: From Silentintroduction, Moodymann's 1997 debut album on Carl Craig's Planet E. Kenny Dixon Jr. loops soul and disco until it becomes hypnotic, and this track is a cornerstone of Detroit's raw, sample-based house.

title: Techno Music
label: 10 Records
note: Juan Atkins's track for the 1988 UK compilation Techno! The New Dance Sound of Detroit. That compilation gave the Detroit sound its name in Britain, and Atkins put the word right into the title.

title: Sharevari
note: A 1981 record made for Detroit's high-school party scene by A Number of Names. Its synth-driven sound is often cited as a forerunner of Detroit techno, arriving before Cybotron's first single.
